items.title: Store the real traceback in build_error_result
items.body:
### Problem

A failed task's error result carries a `traceback` field, but it is always the string `'NoneType: None\n'` instead of the real traceback:

```python
from huey import MemoryHuey
from huey.exceptions import TaskException

huey = MemoryHuey(results=True)

@huey.task()
def boom():
    raise ValueError('kapow')

r = boom()
huey.execute(huey.dequeue())
try:
    r.get()
except TaskException as e:
    print(repr(e.metadata['traceback']))   # "'NoneType: None\n'"
```

`error` and `task_id` are correct — only the traceback is lost. Every failed task is affected.

### Cause

`Huey.build_error_result` fills the field with `traceback.format_exc()`:

```python
def build_error_result(self, task, exception):
    tb = traceback.format_exc()
    ...
```

but it is called from `_execute` *after* the `try/except` that handled the task's exception has already completed. In Python 3, `traceback.format_exc()` reflects the currently-handled exception only while inside the `except` block; once control leaves the handler `sys.exc_info()` is cleared, so it returns `'NoneType: None'`. (The `logger.exception(...)` call logs the real traceback because it runs inside the handler — the stored result does not.)

### Fix

Format the exception's own `__traceback__`, which doesn't depend on being inside a handler:

```python
tb = ''.join(traceback.format_exception(
    type(exception), exception, exception.__traceback__))
```

This is the same approach the Django contrib backend already uses (`huey/contrib/djhuey/tasks_backend.py`).

### Tests

Extended `test_api.py::test_task_error` to assert the stored `metadata['traceback']` contains the error class and message. It fails on `master` (`'NoneType: None\n'`) and passes with the fix.

items.title: How to create a dead-letter-queue for tasks that can't be executed?
items.body:
Hey, I've been having fun where sometime we run into a task that's scheduled but which can't be run.

As an example of how this can happen, suppose that you schedule a task to persistent storage but then delete the code that would actually run it and restart the Huey workers.  Now there's a scheduled task that can't run and which will throw an exception when it gets to here.  It'll also stay on the queue, which means the scheduler will keep trying to rerun it. 
https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/master/huey/registry.py#L49

(Other ways this could happen include things like a bad custom serializer/deserializer, etc.)

What's the right way to catch errors such as this and make sure that tasks which're in that state don't stay queued?

If it's of any use, I'm happy to send a patch for [api.py:deserialize_task()](https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/master/huey/api.py#L299) to add a callback for if a task can't be deserialized?  That way people could decide what to do with it themselves?

> Warning Huey does not guarantee at-least-once delivery of messages, and does not do acknowledgement of completed tasks. items.title: About SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGKILL
items.body:
Hi, not really an issue, but rather a question/doubt about how these signals work in the context of Huey.

I've been reading the docs and other issues, and my current understanding is:
1. Outside of Huey:
  * SIGINT/SIGTERM are used to request a process termination, thus they are mechanisms through which one can implement a graceful shutdown.
  * SIGKILL on the other hand, terminates it on the spot, leaving no space for cleanup.
2. Within Huey:
  * SIGINT is used to request process termination, which allows for extra graceful shutdown (i.e. workers are allowed to finish the tasks they are working on, but no new tasks will be started).
  * SIGTERM is used to "force" the termination of the workers (i.e tasks that are currently executing will end abruptly, and of course, no new tasks will be started). I say "force" (between quotes) because it's not as brute as the SIGKILL signal, because there is some sort of "graceful" shutdown. More concretely, you can execute some cleanup actions, like requeuing the task in order to retry it later. One would do this by adding a handler to the `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` Huey signal (do not confuse with OS signals).
  * SIGKILL is not handled by Huey (and can't be by definition of that signal). Usually one would expect a SIGKILL coming after a SIGTERM, therefore, whatever cleanup task you do within your `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` handler, you better make sure it's fast.

Note: I only mentioned what happens with the worker processes/threads, and left aside the main process and the scheduler process (which are also part of the Huey consumer), because for now I'm only concerned about the workers.

Having said that, my question is: is my understanding correct? Particularly around using a `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` handler to requeue a task that was abruptly ended.

Note: I'm concerned about what would happend in the context of a deployment, where the cloud provider I use sends first a SIGTERM and then a SIGKILL (30 seconds later). I don't mind that the running tasks aren't able to finish in that same execution, so I don't really need to capture the SIGTERM sent by the OS, and transform it into a SIGINT before passing it down to Huey. For me, ending the tasks abruptly, but requeuing them for a later retry is enough.

Let me know what you think, and thanks for building such a great product!

items.title: How to wait on a group of tasks with Huey
items.body:
I'd like to migrate from Celery to Huey but there is one potential sticking point. With Celery, I have a task that spawns a bunch of parallel tasks (a [group](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/userguide/canvas.html#groups)) and waits on all of those parallel tasks to finish before executing a callback using a [chord](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/userguide/canvas.html#chords). For context, the parallel tasks fetch something from an external API, then the callback batch inserts this data into my Postgres database. 

I'm trying to think of how to accomplish something similar with Huey and came up with the following:
1. Just have each task execute an API call and insert the result into the database individually. This is the simplest but potentially hammers the database if a bunch of API calls return simultaneously.
2. Have a master task that spawns a bunch of API call tasks as well as another task that checks the result of all those tasks with a backoff delay.

I'm not really satisfied with either of these approaches and was hoping someone might have a better suggestion.

Add Write-Ahead Log option to SQLite storage
items.body:
This adds an option to enable [Write-Ahead Log](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html) journal for SQLite storage. It provides more concurrent SQLite reads and writes reducing the frequency of "database is locked" type of exceptions.

Some notes:

- `self.sql('pragma journal_mode=%s' % ("WAL" if self._wal else "delete"))` statement is outside the context manager due to `sqlite3.OperationalError: cannot change into wal mode from within a transaction`.
- Looks like WAL mode was available but was lost over time: https://github.com/coleifer/huey/pull/53

items.title: Database corruption with Django & SQLite
items.body:
In trying to emulate Celery's ability to dynamically schedule periodic tasks (#277), I setup some Django models. `RecurringModel` is a singleton, from which Django models that have a `recur` method inherit, and can then be de/-activated in the Django Admin. In order to emulate dynamic periodicity, these models save their execution time info on themselves, as well as the result of their `recur` method, via the standard `save()` method of Django models. Two huey processes are run, one for crontab scheduling (checking every minute for available models) and one for actually running the `recur` methods.

It seems that the setup generally works (the `run_huey --no-periodic` process does the work, while the `--workers=0` process just schedules), but when multiple objects are run, they end up "sharing" data; i.e.: a result of one object's `recur` will be saved on another, despite using the `db_task` decorators.


Am I crazy? Is this too complicated, or missing an important detail?


Periodic scheduler queue (to farm out workers):
`python manage.py run_huey --workers=0`

Worker queue (to run task methods on Django objects):
`python manage.py run_huey --no-periodic --workers=5`

Scheduler & worker tasks: `tasks.py`
```python
@db_task(name='call_recurring_obj')
def call_recurring_obj(obj):
    """ Should run on worker queue """
    obj.recur()

@db_periodic_task(crontab(minute='*'), name='scheduler_minutely')
def scheduler_minutely():
    run_dt = now()
    models = RecurringModel.get_children()
    for model in models:
        objs = model.objects.active()
        for obj in objs.iterator():
            run_dt_range = run_dt + timedelta(seconds=SECONDS_RANGE)
            if not obj.recur_next or run_dt_range > obj.recur_next:
                call_recurring_obj(obj)
            else:
                logger.debug(f"HUEY| Skipping object: {obj}, recurrence in the future: {obj.recur_next}")
```

Django settings: `settings.py`
```python
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3',
        'NAME': os.path.join(DATABASE_DIR, f"{PROJECT_NAME}.db"),
    },
}
HUEY = {
    'name': PROJECT_NAME,
    'result_store': True,  # Store return values of tasks.
    'events': True,  # Consumer emits events allowing real-time monitoring.
    'store_none': False,  # If a task returns None, do not save to results.
    'always_eager': False,
    'store_errors': False,
    'blocking': False,  # Poll the queue rather than do blocking pop.
    'backend_class': 'huey.contrib.sqlitedb.SqliteHuey',
    'connection': {
        'filename': os.path.join(DATABASE_DIR, 'huey.db'),
    },
    'consumer': {
        'workers': HUEY_WORKERS,
        'worker_type': 'thread',
        'initial_delay': 0.1,  # Smallest polling interval, same as -d.
        'backoff': 1.15,  # Exponential backoff using this rate, -b.
        'max_delay': 5, #10.0,  # Max possible polling interval, -m.
        'utc': True,  # Treat ETAs and schedules as UTC datetimes.
        'scheduler_interval': 1,  # Check schedule every second, -s.
        'periodic': True,  # Enable crontab feature.
        'check_worker_health': False, #True,  # Enable worker health checks.
        'health_check_interval': 1,  # Check worker health every second.
        'logger': "huey.consumer",

```

items.title: retry without logging an "unhandled exception"
items.body:
There are some situations where I use Huey and I want a task to be tried, but I don't want an error logged in my logging system because the error is being "handled", it's just the handling involves a retry. 

Adding the error to the logging system pollutes my logs and hides real unhandled errors. 

For example, I use Huey to make API calls against a system. Due to some timing issues, the API call may fail now, but will pass in the future, so I retry the task later. The failure, however, is totally normal and expected. But the only way to get Huey to retry later is to let the exception bubble up, which logs the error, even though it is an expected condition. 

As another example, I fail to get a lock on some resource, and I can't run the task. There is no exception here, I just need to retry later. But the only way is to make up a new exception and raise it, again, filling up the logs with errors that are perfectly normal. 

Probably the easiest solution I can propose is to add a new exception that tasks can raise like `RetryException`, which would cause a retry to occur, but would not be logged as an unhandled exception. I can provide a patch for this if the idea is approved.

items.title: Make redis_backend.py reconnect on database failure
items.body:
Currently if the connection to the database is lost, for any reason... Huey doesn't exit or reconnect to the database. It simply hangs.  
This change, while perhaps not the worlds best way to do it allows Huey to attempt to reconnect to the database should anything happen  

This includes socket timeout, database restart, network failure. All cases where connection is lost, Huey will attempt to reconnect.  
This change still allows for different database configurations for each class, and still attempts to only have a single active connection per class.

Let me know if you have a problem with it and I can attempt to do it another way.

items.title: Disable worker thread
items.body:
This issue is more informational than an actual bug fix. I was hoping to get some feedback and/or support to see if what I'm doing makes sense.

Basically, I ran into a problem during a restart of my consumer process. When the consumer has delegated work to the queue and the worker_pool has delegated the task to a worker thread, it appears that the work is lost when the shutdown method is called.

I've added the `synchronize` example to test.

Without the fix (8a3c255) you can reproduce the issue by starting `consume.py` and `produce.py` in different terminals. While consuming, Ctrl-C the `consume.py` process to stop work. Then, restart the process.

You should observe that the `produce.py` process does not get a result and raises a `huey.exceptions.DataStoreTimeout`. Also, the `consume.py` logs should show that not all work is complete. There should be 0-10 test queries to yahoo and 0-10 test queries to google but depending on where you stopped the consumer, the request is not made.

With a change (45b4d9a) and following the same procedure as above, you should see that all work is completed and the `produce.py` process completes normally.

The change adds an option to disable thread workers. This means that work is completed within the worker_pool thread and that `self._pool` is acquired after `shutdown` is called.

I'm not sure if this is the best approach but it solves the issue I'm having.

Thoughts, ideas, changes?
